reference: Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby/Elsevier.

stations.title: Trace the signal from patient to display

study.intro: A displayed PSG channel is the end of a pathway, not the beginning. When a waveform changes, start with the physiologic source and follow the acquisition path before changing a display setting.
points: Begin with the physiologic source and the sensor or electrode that converts or carries that signal into the recording system.
Follow the channel through the input or headbox pathway, amplification and acquisition electronics, digital conversion, software, display, and storage as the specific system is designed.
Different manufacturers place amplification, conversion, and ancillary devices in different physical locations, so use the system documentation rather than assuming one universal hardware order.
Separate a display-only change from a change that alters acquired or stored data; the same screen appearance can have very different consequences for later review.

visual.label: Original SPG schematic tracing a physiologic signal through patient interface, acquisition hardware, software, display, and storage.

apply.prompt: One EEG channel becomes flat while neighboring EEG channels and the rest of the study remain stable. What is the best first troubleshooting direction?
options: Increase the high-frequency filter until the flat channel looks active
Trace that channel from its electrode and lead through its input pathway before changing acquisition settings
Reconfigure every respiratory channel because the problem may be systemic
Assume the patient stopped producing cerebral activity in one derivation
apply.answer: Trace that channel from its electrode and lead through its input pathway before changing acquisition settings
apply.hint: A problem limited to one channel usually deserves a local pathway check before a system-wide setting change.
apply.rationale: A single-channel failure is most efficiently approached by tracing that channel's local patient-to-input pathway before altering filters or other acquisition settings.

recap.reviewed: Patient-to-display signal flow, system variation, local pathway checks, and display-versus-storage changes.
recap.canDo: Follow a questionable waveform backward through the acquisition pathway instead of treating the screen as the source of the problem.

study.intro: A PSG derivation represents a relationship between inputs. Understanding which channels share a reference makes it possible to predict which channels should change together when one reference pathway is disturbed.
points: A displayed bioelectric derivation depends on the potential difference between its selected inputs; changing the input relationship changes the waveform that is displayed.
Reversing the two inputs reverses the displayed polarity without reversing the patient's underlying physiology.
A disturbance at a shared reference can appear simultaneously in every derivation that uses that reference while independent derivations remain comparatively clean.
Use channel relationships to localize the problem: shared-reference contamination should follow the reference, not every channel in the montage.

visual.label: Original SPG reference-tree schematic comparing M2-referenced channels with independent M1 and bipolar pathways.

apply.prompt: F3-M2, C3-M2, E1-M2, and E2-M2 develop the same disturbance, while F4-M1, C4-M1, chin EMG, and ECG remain comparatively clean. Which pathway should be inspected first?
options: The shared M2 reference pathway
The chin EMG bipolar pair
Every respiratory sensor simultaneously
The M1 reference because the M1 channels are the cleanest
apply.hint: Look for the component shared only by the channels that changed together.
apply.rationale: The disturbed channels all use M2, while independent M1-referenced and bipolar channels remain comparatively clean. That pattern localizes the first check to the shared M2 pathway.

recap.reviewed: Input relationships, polarity, referential versus independent pathways, and shared-reference localization.
recap.canDo: Use the pattern of affected derivations to distinguish a local channel problem from a shared-reference disturbance.

study.intro: Differential amplifiers emphasize the difference between two inputs while reducing signals that arrive similarly at both inputs. Electrode quality and balance influence how well this works in real recordings.
points: The amplifier should preserve the physiologic difference between its inputs while reducing unwanted signals that are common to both.
Low, reasonably balanced electrode impedances support effective rejection of environmental interference across a derivation.
Marked impedance imbalance can make a channel more vulnerable to line-frequency and other common environmental noise.
Correct the patient-electrode and lead pathway before using a notch filter or other setting to cosmetically hide preventable interference.

visual.label: Original SPG schematic showing two inputs carrying shared noise plus a smaller differential physiologic signal.

apply.prompt: A derivation develops strong line-frequency interference and its two electrode impedances are markedly unequal. What should the technologist do first?
options: Correct and rebalance the electrode contacts, then reassess the channel
Apply the strongest available notch filter and leave the electrodes unchanged
Increase display gain so the interference occupies more of the screen
Delete the derivation from the montage
apply.answer: Correct and rebalance the electrode contacts, then reassess the channel
apply.hint: Common-mode rejection depends on the quality and balance of the two input pathways.
apply.rationale: Marked impedance imbalance can weaken rejection of common interference. Correcting the electrode pathways addresses the source before filtering is considered.

recap.reviewed: Differential amplification, common-mode rejection, impedance balance, and line-frequency susceptibility.
recap.canDo: Recognize when a noisy derivation should be repaired at the inputs instead of hidden with a filter.

stations.title: Sensitivity, gain, calibration, and display scale

study.intro: The height of a waveform on the screen is not the same thing as the size of the physiologic signal. Sensitivity, gain, scale, and calibration determine how recorded voltage is represented visually.
points: Changing sensitivity, gain, or display scale can make the same underlying signal appear taller or shorter without changing the patient.
Calibration provides a known reference response that helps verify the relationship between signal amplitude and the recording system.
When amplitude changes abruptly, check whether a setting changed before assuming the patient's physiology changed by the same amount.
Know whether the system applies a change only to the current display or commits it to acquisition or stored data.

visual.label: Original SPG schematic showing the same underlying waveform displayed at two different vertical scales.

apply.prompt: An EEG waveform suddenly appears much taller immediately after the display sensitivity was changed, but timing and morphology are otherwise unchanged. What should be checked before calling this a physiologic amplitude increase?
options: The sensitivity or gain/display-scale setting and whether the change was display-only or stored
Whether the patient entered REM solely because the waveform is taller
Whether the pulse oximeter needs a new sampling rate
Whether every electrode should be replaced
apply.answer: The sensitivity or gain/display-scale setting and whether the change was display-only or stored
apply.hint: Displayed height depends on both the recorded signal and the scale used to show it.
apply.rationale: A settings change can alter displayed amplitude without an equivalent physiologic change. Verify the scale and how the system applies that change before interpreting amplitude.

recap.reviewed: Displayed amplitude, sensitivity/gain, calibration, and display-only versus stored changes.
recap.canDo: Separate a true signal-amplitude change from a change caused by the way the system displays the signal.

study.intro: Filters change which frequency components remain prominent in a recorded channel. They can improve readability, but excessive filtering can also remove or distort clinically important waveform components.
points: A low-frequency filter attenuates components below the selected range, while a high-frequency filter attenuates components above the selected range.
Filter changes affect waveform shape and amplitude, so they should be made deliberately and within current technical guidance and facility policy.
A display filter may change only what the technologist sees, whereas another system setting may alter data that are stored or later reviewed.
Do not use filtering as the first response to an electrode, movement, sweat, or hardware problem that can be corrected at its source.

visual.label: Original SPG frequency schematic comparing a mixed signal with slow components attenuated and fast components attenuated.

apply.prompt: A channel develops large slow baseline drift after the patient becomes warm and sweaty. What is the best first response?
options: Inspect and correct the electrode/site and other likely artifact sources before changing filters
Raise the low-frequency filter aggressively until the drift disappears
Lower the high-frequency filter to remove the slow drift
Change the sleep stage so the drift is no longer considered artifact
apply.answer: Inspect and correct the electrode/site and other likely artifact sources before changing filters
apply.hint: A filter can alter the appearance without correcting the physical cause of the artifact.
apply.rationale: Slow drift should prompt a source check first. Aggressive filtering can attenuate legitimate slow components and make the channel look cleaner without repairing the recording pathway.

recap.reviewed: Low- and high-frequency attenuation, filter-related distortion, and source-first artifact correction.
recap.canDo: Predict the general effect of a filter change and avoid using filters to conceal a correctable signal problem.

study.intro: Digital PSG represents continuous physiologic signals with discrete samples. The acquisition rate must be high enough to represent the fastest signal component of interest without creating misleading lower-frequency aliases.
points: Sampling rate is expressed as samples per second and determines how densely the original signal is represented in digital data.

As a minimum mathematical principle, the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency that must be represented; practical systems may sample higher to improve reconstruction and reduce aliasing risk.
Too few samples can blunt or distort a waveform, and aliasing can make high-frequency content appear falsely at lower frequencies.

Higher sampling increases data volume, so channel settings should follow current technical guidance, manufacturer capability, and facility policy rather than simply using the maximum value everywhere.

visual.label: Original SPG schematic comparing dense digital samples with undersampling of the same continuous waveform.

apply.prompt: A digital channel is configured with a sampling rate below twice the highest frequency the channel is expected to represent. What is the primary signal-integrity risk?
options: Aliasing and distortion of the reconstructed waveform
Improved common-mode rejection
Automatic correction of electrode impedance
Reversal of recording polarity
apply.answer: Aliasing and distortion of the reconstructed waveform
apply.hint: Think about what happens when the system takes too few snapshots of a changing signal.
apply.rationale: Undersampling can misrepresent higher-frequency content and create aliases in the reconstructed signal. Acquisition sampling should be adequate for the intended bandwidth.

recap.reviewed: Sampling rate, waveform reconstruction, aliasing, and the tradeoff between resolution and data volume.
recap.canDo: Recognize an undersampling risk and explain why adequate acquisition sampling matters before display or scoring.

stations.title: Troubleshoot, correct, and document the pathway

study.intro: Efficient troubleshooting uses the pattern of failure. One abnormal channel suggests a local pathway; several related channels changing together suggests a component they share.
points: Compare affected and unaffected channels before touching settings; the pattern often identifies whether the problem is local, shared, or system-wide.
Follow the most likely path from patient interface through lead, connector/input, reference, amplifier/acquisition pathway, software, and display as appropriate to the equipment.
Restore the physiologic signal instead of making a cosmetic display change that hides the defect.
Document what changed, what was checked or corrected, whether data quality was affected, and any unresolved limitation that matters to later review.

visual.label: Original SPG decision schematic separating one-channel, shared-reference, and broader acquisition failures.

apply.prompt: Several related bioelectric channels fail together while respiratory device channels continue normally. Which approach is most efficient?
options: Inspect the shared bioelectric reference/input/amplifier pathway before reworking unrelated respiratory sensors
Replace every sensor on the patient at once
Apply stronger filters to all channels without checking the hardware pattern
Ignore the failure because some channels are still recording
apply.answer: Inspect the shared bioelectric reference/input/amplifier pathway before reworking unrelated respiratory sensors
apply.hint: Use what the affected channels have in common to narrow the search.
apply.rationale: A simultaneous failure limited to related bioelectric channels points first to a shared component in that pathway, not to independent respiratory device channels.

recap.reviewed: Pattern-based troubleshooting, local versus shared failures, source correction, and documentation.
recap.canDo: Localize a signal failure efficiently and leave a clear record of the corrective action and remaining data-quality limits.
